126 = 13 + 113 (or 19 + 107)
128 = 19 + 109 (or 31 + 97)
Each even number between 120 and 130 is written as the sum of two prime numbers.

steps.explain: List all the even numbers strictly between 120 and 130.
Identify prime numbers close to this range that can be used as components.
Decompose each even number into a sum of two primes. Check every component IS actually prime — a common wrong-option trick uses \(111=3\times37\) or \(115=5\times23\), which are composite, not prime.
All components used (13, 109, 11, 113, 19) are verified prime numbers, confirming Goldbach's conjecture for these values.

questions.stem: Explain why a square number has an odd number of factors, and a non-square number has an even number of factors. Which explanation is correct?
options: Factors always pair up so that \(a \times b = N\). For a non-square \(N\), every factor \(a\) has a distinct partner \(b \ne a\), so factors come in complete pairs (an even total). For a square \(N\), the factor \(s=\sqrt{N}\) pairs with itself, contributing only 1 factor instead of 2 — making the total odd.
Square numbers always have exactly 3 factors (1, the square root, and the number itself), which is why the count is odd.
Every number's factors come in pairs, and squares simply have one extra factor added on at the end for no particular reason — it's a coincidence that this makes the count odd.
Non-square numbers have an odd number of factors because their square roots are irrational, while square numbers have an even number of factors because their square roots are whole numbers.
questions.hint: Consider how factors are paired up.
questions.solution:
Factors always occur in pairs that multiply to the number.
For a non-square number, each factor has a distinct partner, so the total count is even.
For a square number, the square root pairs with itself, which only contributes one distinct number, making the total count odd.

steps.explain: Factors can be listed in pairs that multiply to give the number \(N\).
steps.work: \(\text{If } a \times b = N, \text{ then } a \text{ and } b \text{ are a factor pair.}\)

steps.explain: If \(N\) is not a square number, every factor \(a\) has a distinct partner \(b \neq a\). This groups the factors into pairs of size 2.
If \(N\) is a square number, there exists a factor \(s=\sqrt{N}\) such that \(s \times s = N\). This factor pairs with itself.
steps.work: \(\text{Square: } s \text{ pairs with itself} \implies \text{only 1 distinct factor from that pair}\)

steps.explain: Since every other factor pair is still distinct, the self-paired square root makes the total number of distinct factors odd.

questions.stem: Find all possible values of the missing digit \\(x\\) so that the number \\(34,82x\\) is divisible by \\(3\\).
questions.hint: A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.

steps.explain: A number is divisible by 3 if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
Find single digits \\(x\\) from 0 to 9 such that \\(17 + x\\) is a multiple of 3 (18, 21, 24).
steps.work: \\(\begin{aligned} 17 + x &= 18 \implies x = 1 \\ 17 + x &= 21 \implies x = 4 \\ 17 + x &= 24 \implies x = 7 \end{aligned}\\)

questions.stem: Find all possible values of the missing digit \\(x\\) so that the number \\(288x5\\) is divisible by \\(3\\).
questions.hint: Calculate the sum of the digits and check divisibility by 3.

steps.explain: We need \\(23 + x\\) to be divisible by 3. The multiples of 3 larger than 23 are 24, 27, and 30.
steps.work: \\(\begin{aligned} 23 + x &= 24 \implies x = 1 \\ 23 + x &= 27 \implies x = 4 \\ 23 + x &= 30 \implies x = 7 \end{aligned}\\)

questions.stem: Find all possible values of the missing digit \\(x\\) (which cannot be 0) so that the number \\(x47\\) is divisible by \\(3\\).
questions.hint: Calculate digit sum. Note that x is the first digit, so x cannot be 0.

steps.explain: We need \\(x + 11\\) to be a multiple of 3 (12, 15, 18).
steps.work: \\(\begin{aligned} x + 11 &= 12 \implies x = 1 \\ x + 11 &= 15 \implies x = 4 \\ x + 11 &= 18 \implies x = 7 \end{aligned}\\)

questions.stem: Find all possible values of the missing digit \\(x\\) so that the number \\(84,73x\\) is divisible by \\(6\\).

steps.explain: Divisibility by 6 requires the number to be divisible by both 2 and 3. For divisibility by 2, \\(x\\) must be even.
For divisibility by 3, digit sum must be divisible by 3.

Digit sum must be divisible by 3.
For \\(6+x\\) to be a multiple of 3, \\(x\\) must be a multiple of 3.

questions.stem: Find the missing digit \\(x\\) so that the number \\(20x0\\) is divisible by \\(3, 4\\) and \\(5\\).
questions.hint: LCM of 3, 4 and 5 is 60. Ends in 0, so it is divisible by 5. For 4, the last two digits (x0) must be a multiple of 4.

steps.explain: Divisibility by 5 is guaranteed since the last digit is 0. For divisibility by 4, the last two digits \\(x0\\) must be divisible by 4.
For divisibility by 3, digit sum must be divisible by 3.
Test candidates: 2+0=2, 2+2=4, 2+4=6 (yes!), 2+6=8, 2+8=10. The only valid digit is 4.

steps.explain: For divisibility by 5, the last digit \\(x\\) must be 0 or 5. But for divisibility by 4, it must be even, so \\(x\\) must be 0.

questions.stem: Find the missing digit \\(x\\) so that the number \\(34x20\\) is divisible by \\(11\\).

We need \\(x - 3\\) to be divisible by 11. Since \\(x\\) is a digit (0 to 9), the only way is if the sum is 0.
